original_target.title: Do bounded minimal graphs over the hyperbolic disk have radial limits almost everywhere?
original_target.area: Geometric analysis and boundary behavior of nonlinear elliptic equations

full_original_statement:
Let $`D=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<1\}`$ carry the complete hyperbolic metric $`g=4|dz|^2/(1-|z|^2)^2`$. Suppose $`u\in C^2(D)`$ is bounded and its graph in $`(D,g)\times\mathbb R`$ is minimal; equivalently,

```math
\mathrm{div}_g\!\left(\frac{\nabla_g u}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla_g u|_g^2}}\right)=0.
```


**Must $`\lim_{r\uparrow1}u(re^{i\theta})`$ exist for Lebesgue-almost every $`\theta\in[0,2\pi)`$?** Boundedness makes any existing limit finite. An entire bounded minimal graph with no radial limit on a set of positive angular measure would refute the conjecture.

sources.scope_comparison: The exact target is bounded minimal graphs over the complete hyperbolic disk with radial limits almost everywhere. The primary paper explicitly retains this bounded hyperbolic conjecture. Section 3's positive theorem is for the Euclidean unit ball, while Section 2's hyperbolic example has unbounded heights after reflected extensions; neither proves nor refutes the bounded target. Focused later resolution and announcement searches did not locate a theorem removing this distinction.
